title: Why Surprise Matters in Teacher CPD: What the Hypercorrection Effect Can Teach Us About Better Professional Learning
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes argues that most teacher CPD fails not because its content is wrong but because information alone rarely revises professional judgement, leaving teachers to comply briefly and then revert. Her move is to borrow the hypercorrection effect from learning research: when someone is confident and wrong, the correction lands harder and sticks longer than when they were merely unsure. Surprise, she says, is the felt signal that a mental model has failed, and it does three jobs at once by capturing attention, surfacing the assumption, and opening the door to revision. She is careful to fence this off from 'gotcha CPD' - productive surprise only works inside psychological safety, where being wrong is normal and the aim is improvement rather than exposure. The piece then turns practical, working the idea through three worked cases (retrieval practice, written feedback, cold calling) and proposing a Predict-Reveal-Explain-Adapt-Revisit design sequence, with the point that no prediction means no surprise. It closes with five failure modes for facilitators, including surprise as theatre and treating evidence as self-explanatory. The underlying claim is that CPD is the refinement of professional judgement, not the delivery of techniques.
points: The design principle worth stealing is that teachers must commit to a prediction before the reveal, because without a prediction there is no prediction error and therefore no productive surprise.

Hughes distinguishes technique-led CPD from judgement-led CPD: techniques framed as commandments produce robotic teaching, while techniques framed as conditional tools invite diagnosis, principle and adaptation.

Her list of facilitator failure modes is the most reusable part - dramatic reveals without explanatory follow-through, contradiction mistaken for learning, and too many corrections at once all convert surprise into noise.
The hypercorrection mechanism only pays off under psychological safety; used to catch teachers out, the same technique destroys trust and shuts learning down.
Because a strong first encoding is not durable change, she insists on a Revisit step through coaching, departmental meetings or low-stakes quizzes.
quotes: There’s a version of CPD that leaves teachers with a page of strategies and very little change in practice. The ideas may be sensible. The delivery may be polished.
That moment of confident error creates a jolt. It interrupts autopilot. It exposes a hidden assumption.

In practical terms, that means a teacher who is mildly unsure and gets corrected may learn something. But a teacher who is certain and then discovers they’re mistaken may learn it more deeply, because the correction lands harder.
That is why surprise can be such a high-leverage tool in professional development. It is not just about engagement. It is about conceptual change.
If leaders or facilitators treat surprise as a way to catch teachers out, embarrass them, or perform expertise, it destroys trust and shuts learning down. People become defensive, not reflective.
At its best, CPD is not the delivery of techniques. It is the refinement of professional judgement.
